- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files.     14	# Artifact type: process-definition
    15	
    16	## Identity and ancestry
    17

    26	
    27	## Required frontmatter
    28	
    29	`type: process-definition`, `id`, `owner`, `status`, `created`,
    30	`updated`; `produces` (artifact
    31	types a run creates; the generic root `definition` covers runs creating

    38	conversation); `ask-cap` (ISO 8601 duration — how long an ask may stand
    39	unanswered before its default applies; required for any process whose
    40	steps carry `asks`).

    42	## Required sections
    43	
    44	1. **Purpose** — one short paragraph.
    45	2. **Guiding statement** (optional) — directs judgment across the whole
    46	   process; the compiler copies it into every rendering.

    48	4. **Roles** — roles and their accountability; role files carry identity,
    49	   never sequencing.
    50	5. **Flow (compiled)** — the diagram generated from the steps; never
    51	   edited by hand.
    52	6. **Data** — process-local value names. Simple types (JSON Schema
    53	   primitives) inline; every structured shape is a `$ref` to a defined
    54	   type with an explicit source: `from:` is a relative link to the
    55	   defining file, or `pkg:<package>/<type>` when the type lives in
    56	   another package and is fetched through that package's contract tool
    57	   (e.g. `shop-knowledge schema session-record`). Every distinct `$ref`
    58	   carries `from:` at least once; the linter verifies local sources
    59	   define the referenced type. No structured shape is ever defined here.
    60	   A value may declare `initial` — its value at run start.
    61	7. **Steps** — the executable part (shape below).

    67	artifact-typedef rule).

    70	
    71	Top-level keys: `start` (first step id); optional `parameters` (data
    72	values supplied at instantiation rather than produced by any step);
    73	optional `result` (the data value a run returns — the artifact, not a

   107	## Run lifecycle
   108	
   109	A run is one execution of a process, anchored to a work item in the

    13	
    14	## Purpose
    15	
    16	A question one activity puts to another role, returned by an agent or
    17	human step in place of its output. Produced by any step whose process
    18	lists it under `asks`; consumed by the runtime, which holds the run,
    19	routes the ask to the named role, and re-enters the step with the

    25	role owes; the `kind` field names which. The `checkpoint` carries the
    26	asker's partial output so the resume repeats no work. A `clarify` is an

13	    12	# Base writing style
14	    13	
15	    14	These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
16	    15	document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
17	    16	never override it.
18	    17	
19	    18	## Goal
20	    19	
21	    20	The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
22	    21	seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.
23	    22	
24	    23	## Lead with the point
25	    24	
26	    25	At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.
27	    26	
28	    27	- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
29	    28	- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
30	    29	- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.
31	    30	
32	    31	If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
33	    32	applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
34	    33	one.
35	    34	
36	    35	## Detail placement
37	    36	
38	    37	Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
39	    38	language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
40	    39	claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.
41	    40	
42	    41	## Sentences
43	    42	
44	    43	- One idea per sentence.
45	    44	- Active voice, with a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks,"
46	    45	  not "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
47	    46	- Prefer the short common word: "use" not "utilize," "end" not
48	    47	  "terminate," "before" not "prior to."
49	    48	
50	    49	## Terminology
51	    50	
52	    51	- Never use a metaphor as a technical term. If a word describes a thing
53	    52	  by what it resembles instead of what it literally does, replace it with
54	    53	  the literal description. Test: could a competent reader from outside
55	    54	  the team work out the meaning from the words alone? If not, rewrite.
56	    55	- Banned words. Never use these, in any form:
57	    56	  - "load-bearing" → say "other work depends on it" or "critical to
58	    57	    operations"
59	    58	  - "surface" (as in context surface, config surface) → say "input,"
60	    59	    "source," or "channel"
61	    60	  - "seam" → say "boundary" or "integration point"
62	    61	  - "scar tissue" → describe the actual problem, e.g. "an unreviewed
63	    62	    workaround that was never removed"
64	    63	- Explain every insider reference — a past incident, an internal system,
65	    64	  a person — in one plain sentence, or cut it. Assume the reader knows
66	    65	  none of our history.
67	    66	
68	    67	## Style examples
69	    68	
70	    69	These examples exist only to show sentence style. The domain (a public
71	    70	library) is deliberately unrelated to our work. Copy the style; never
72	    71	copy the content or vocabulary into real documents.
73	    72	
74	    73	bad:
75	    74	
76	    75	> Unreturned inventory constitutes scar tissue on the circulation loop
77	    76	> and rapidly becomes load-bearing for downstream shelving throughput.
78	    77	
79	    78	good:
80	    79	
81	    80	> Overdue books pile up at the front desk, and staff spend their time
82	    81	> reshelving late returns instead of helping visitors.
83	    82	
84	    83	The bad sentence uses two metaphors as terms and never names an actor.
85	    84	The good sentence says who is affected and what actually happens, in
86	    85	plain words.

308	    19	  process: what it is for, what a run produces, and every step in a form
309	    20	  a runtime can construct a workflow from. Skills, flow
310	    21	  diagrams, and fabro graphs (fabro is the fleet's workflow-orchestrator

346	    57	   (e.g. `shop-knowledge schema session-record`). Every distinct `$ref`
347	    58	   carries `from:` at least once; the linter verifies local sources
348	    59	   define the referenced type. No structured shape is ever defined here.
349	    60	   A value may declare `initial` — its value at run start.
350	    61	7. **Steps** — the executable part (shape below).
351	    62	8. **Derived checks** — a table: outcome, check, kind, where; every row
352	    63	   cites its clause or is deleted.
353	    64	
354	    65	Header elements 1–4 are bolded labels before the first heading; 5–8 are
355	    66	markdown headings in order (a section is a heading, per the
356	    67	artifact-typedef rule).
357	    68	
358	    69	## The steps section
359	    70	
360	    71	Top-level keys: `start` (first step id); optional `parameters` (data
361	    72	values supplied at instantiation rather than produced by any step);
362	    73	optional `result` (the data value a run returns — the artifact, not a
363	    74	status record; omit only when the outcomes pin the run's value). `end`
364	    75	is the reserved terminator id for `next`. Each step:
365	    76	
366	    77	- `id`, `name`; `run-by` — `{role, execution: agent}`,
367	    78	  `{role, execution: human}` (a role a person holds, e.g. an authority review), or `{execution: runtime}`; `fresh-context: true` where a role
368	    79	  must not carry memory between runs.
369	    80	- `inputs` / `outputs` — lists of declared data names; the typed contract
370	    81	  is the isolation mechanism (a step reads only what it lists).
371	    82	- Agent and human steps carry `prompt` — **the only prose allowed in a
372	    83	  step** (for a human step it is the review's ask).
373	    84	- Runtime steps carry `set` (CEL assignments to data values or their
374	    85	  fields), `run` (command templates
375	    86	  with `${...}` interpolation from typed inputs; `atomic: true` binds the
376	    87	  lines into one all-or-nothing act), or `branches`.
377	    88	- `checks` — CEL expressions over declared data.
378	    89	- Routing: `next`, or `branches` of `{label, when (CEL), next}` rows plus
379	    90	  one `else`. **Every loop declares its exits as labeled branch rows** —
380	    91	  a reached-state success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
381	    92	- `asks` — optional list of role ids the step may put an ask to (the
382	    93	  [`ask`](../types/ask.md) data type). An agent or human step listed
383	    94	  with `asks` may return an ask in place of its outputs; a step without
384	    95	  `asks` may not ask. Every ask names a `default` and a `checkpoint`; the
385	    96	  step's prompt states what kind of information it may ask for — never
386	    97	  a judgment the step's role owes. Steps that frame or plan ask early;
387	    98	  an ask from a producing step wastes the work not in its checkpoint.
388	    99	- `annotations` — per-step rendering metadata keyed by target (e.g.
389	   100	  `fabro: {model, max_attempts}`); the definition itself ignores them.
390	   101	- `run-by: {execution: sub-process, process: <process-id>, from: <source>}`
391	   102	  runs another process definition as one step: the step's inputs map to
392	   103	  the child's parameters and its outputs receive the child's result. A
393	   104	  conversation invoked this way is a branched conversation: the child's
394	   105	  anchor records the parent run.
395	   106	
396	   107	## Run lifecycle
397	   108	
398	   109	A run is one execution of a process, anchored to a work item in the
399	   110	registry. Run states: `running`, `held`, `done`, `cancelled`.
400	   111	
401	   112	- **Hold** pauses a run: the current step and every data value persist in
402	   113	  the run's anchor, and the work item records the state. A held run is
403	   114	  resumed at its recorded step or cancelled with a reason — never
404	   115	  silently dropped.
405	   116	- The `hold-after` window makes parking automatic: a run with no activity
406	   117	  inside the window is held by the runtime. Unfinished work parks itself
407	   118	  with a named resume point; nothing dangles in the lead repo.
408	   119	- **Ask** holds a run the same way, with the ask recorded on the anchor
409	   120	  and routed to whoever fills the role it names — a person or an agent;
410	   121	  the answer is written to the ask and the run resumes at the asking
411	   122	  step with the ask in its inputs, in a fresh context loaded from the
412	   123	  step's declared inputs and the checkpoint. There is no synchronous
413	   124	  form: no step waits in place for an answer. An unanswered ask resolves
414	   125	  to its `default` at the process's `ask-cap` (an ISO 8601 duration,
415	   126	  required for any process whose steps carry `asks`), and the run
416	   127	  resumes on the default with the ask marked `defaulted`. An ask that
417	   128	  recurs across runs is a gap in a definition; the answering role files
418	   129	  the definition change, and the ask stops.
419	   130	- **Cancel** closes the run's work item with a reason and files the
420	   131	  resulting actions the outcomes demand.
421	   132	
422	   133	## Rendering contract
423	   134	
424	   135	The compiler generates: the in-document flow diagram (typed inputs and
425	   136	outputs on every node; the result on the end node) and the skill —
426	   137	front-matter (`generated: true`, `generated-by`, `derived-from`,
427	   138	`source`, `source-digest`) and body (purpose, guiding statement, result,
428	   139	diagram, one section per step with the prompt verbatim). Conformance
429	   140	check: re-run the compiler and diff.
430	   141	
431	   142	## Commitment (Definition of Done)
432	   143	
433	   144	A process definition is done when it compiles — every `$ref` resolves,
434	   145	the diagram and renderings generate, `result` (if declared) names a data
435	   146	value — and every loop declares its exit. **Consequence on failure:** it
436	   147	cannot be dispatched, carried by a skill, or cited by a check.
437	   148	
438	   149	## Sources
439	   150	
440	   151	ISO/IEC/IEEE 24774 (name/purpose/outcomes header); GitHub Actions (step
441	   152	records with typed inputs/outputs); CNCF Serverless Workflow
442	   153	(data-condition transitions); CEL — Common Expression Language
443	   154	(mechanically translatable conditions); Essence-style state exits plus a
444	   155	round cap (the dual-exit rule).
445	   156	
446	   157	## Derived review checklist
447	   158	
448	   159	- Compiles clean: refs resolve, diagram and renderings regenerate
449	   160	  byte-stable. *(Commitment)*
450	   161	- No prose inside step records outside `prompt` fields; section
451	   162	  introduction prose is body text, not step content. *(§The steps section)*
452	   163	- Every loop has labeled success and/or cap exits. *(§The steps section)*
453	   164	- Every step with `asks` belongs to a process with `ask-cap`; every ask
454	   165	  names a default and a checkpoint. *(§The steps section, §Run lifecycle)*
455	   166	- Outcomes each name a witness. *(§Required sections 3)*
456	   167	- `result`, if absent, is justified by outcomes that pin the run's value.
457	   168	  *(§The steps section)*

583	    14	
584	    15	These statements govern every activity in this shop. The full set —
585	    16	rationales, implications, fitness screen — is the source document
586	    17	named in the front-matter; on conflict the source wins.
587	    18	
588	    19	- **Define what good looks like up front** (`define-good-up-front`):
589	    20	  - Every activity MUST operate from a stated definition of what good looks like.
590	    21	  - That definition MUST drive both the performance of the activity and its check.
591	    22	  - The check MUST sit with a different role holding a different accountability.
592	    23	- **Govern the generating context** (`governed-context`):
593	    24	  - Everything loaded into an agent's generating context — prompts, skills, memories, primers — MUST trace to an approved definition or a governed record.
594	    25	  - An unsanctioned context channel MUST NOT be created or retained.
595	    26	- **Every activity belongs to a process** (`no-orphan-activities`):
596	    27	  - Every activity in the system MUST be part of a defined process with stated expected outcomes, expected outputs, and possible resulting actions.
597	    28	  - Every long-running loop MUST declare its exit — a reached-state success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
598	    29	- **Use defined terms** (`use-defined-terms`):
599	    30	  - Important terms MUST be defined in the system, in the glossary or as a schema element.
600	    31	  - A term is important when a reader must know it to perform or check the work.
601	    32	  - When more than one term could carry a statement, the writer MUST use a defined term if one is available.
602	    33	- **Use external standards first** (`external-standards-first`):
603	    34	  - A definition MUST adopt an established external form where one fits.
604	    35	  - Bespoke structure MUST be justified by a recorded gap in the form it rejects.
605	    36	- **Single source of truth** (`single-source-of-truth`):
606	    37	  - Every fact, rule, or definition MUST have exactly one authoritative home.
607	    38	  - Every other appearance MUST be a reference or a generated rendering.
608	    39	- **Feedback loops have consumers** (`feedback-loops-with-consumers`):
609	    40	  - Every feedback channel MUST name its consumer and the resulting action.
610	    41	  - The effectiveness of processes, tools, and prompts MUST be measured.
611	    42	  - The definitions of processes, tools, and prompts MUST be updated from what is measured.
612	    43	- **Delivery is verified in the running system** (`delivery-verified`):
613	    44	  - Work MUST be counted done only when its effect is demonstrated in the running system.
614	    45	  - Artifacts existing, checks passing, or reviews approving MUST NOT count as done on their own.
615	    46	- **Load the least context** (`least-context`):
616	    47	  - An activity MUST load the minimum context necessary to accomplish its task.
617	    48	  - The activity's process MUST name what loads into context and the source each input comes from.
618	    49	  - Context from an unapproved source MUST NOT be loaded.

    11	
    12	# Base writing style
    13	
    14	These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
    15	document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
    16	never override it.
    17	
    18	## Goal
    19	
    20	The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
    21	seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.
    22	
    23	## Lead with the point
    24	
    25	At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.
    26	
    27	- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
    28	- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
    29	- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.
    30	
    31	If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
    32	applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
    33	one.
    34	
    35	## Detail placement
    36	
    37	Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
    38	language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
    39	claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.
    40	
    41	## Sentences
    42	
    43	- One idea per sentence.
    44	- Active voice, with a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks,"
    45	  not "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
    46	- Prefer the short common word: "use" not "utilize," "end" not
    47	  "terminate," "before" not "prior to."
    48	
    49	## Terminology
    50	
    51	- Never use a metaphor as a technical term. If a word describes a thing
    52	  by what it resembles instead of what it literally does, replace it with
    53	  the literal description. Test: could a competent reader from outside
    54	  the team work out the meaning from the words alone? If not, rewrite.
    55	- Banned words. Never use these, in any form:
    56	  - "load-bearing" → say "other work depends on it" or "critical to
    57	    operations"
    58	  - "surface" (as in context surface, config surface) → say "input,"
    59	    "source," or "channel"
    60	  - "seam" → say "boundary" or "integration point"
    61	  - "scar tissue" → describe the actual problem, e.g. "an unreviewed
    62	    workaround that was never removed"
    63	- Explain every insider reference — a past incident, an internal system,
    64	  a person — in one plain sentence, or cut it. Assume the reader knows
    65	  none of our history.
    66	
    67	## Style examples
    68	
    69	These examples exist only to show sentence style. The domain (a public
    70	library) is deliberately unrelated to our work. Copy the style; never
    71	copy the content or vocabulary into real documents.
    72	
    73	bad:
    74	
    75	> Unreturned inventory constitutes scar tissue on the circulation loop
    76	> and rapidly becomes load-bearing for downstream shelving throughput.
    77	
    78	good:
    79	
    80	> Overdue books pile up at the front desk, and staff spend their time
    81	> reshelving late returns instead of helping visitors.
    82	
    83	The bad sentence uses two metaphors as terms and never names an actor.
    84	The good sentence says who is affected and what actually happens, in
    85	plain words.
    86

     1	---
     2	type: glossary

    10	---
    11	
    12	# Glossary
    13	
    14	## How the list combines
    15	
    16	The defined-term list is this glossary combined with every schema element
    17	name. Per the `use-defined-terms` principle, a writer choosing between
    18	terms uses one of these when one fits.
    19	
    20	## Terms
    21	
    22	- **artifact type** — a named, schema-defined document type (e.g.
    23	  `decision-brief`); the term the schema registry uses. Not "kind".
    24	- **data type** — a named, schema-defined structure that is not a
    25	  human-readable document (e.g. `review`); passed between process steps.
    26	- **simple type** — a JSON Schema primitive (`string`, `integer`,
    27	  `boolean`, `array`, `object`), usable inline without registration.
    28	- **typedef** — the single source a type is generated from; templates and
    29	  schema fragments are its renderings (owned by shopsystem-knowledge).
    30	- **schema** — the machine-checkable shape of a type: fields, types,
    31	  enums, required sections.
    32	- **process definition** — the source of truth for a process: header
    33	  (purpose, outcomes, roles), data section, steps section.
    34	- **step** — one unit of a process: an agent step (carries a prompt) or a
    35	  runtime step (carries `set`, `run`, or `branches`; no prose).
    36	- **rendering** — a generated output of a definition (a skill, a
    37	  diagram, a template); never edited by hand, never the source of truth.
    38	- **guiding statement** — an optional header element of a process
    39	  definition that directs judgment across the whole process; compiled
    40	  into every rendering.
    41	- **fitness set** — judged (never executed) Given/When/Then scenarios
    42	  scoring an artifact type's quality.
    43	- **guideline** — prose quality rules for an artifact type, each with a
    44	  test, a criterion, and a yes/no decision.
    45	- **role** — a named capability contract and set of accountabilities,
    46	  assigned by process steps to whoever fills it; sequencing lives in
    47	  process definitions, not roles.
    48	- **principle** — a standing rule about how we work: name, statement,
    49	  rationale, implications (see the principles document's opening
    50	  definition).
    51	- **seed layer** — the hand-approved definitions the regress terminates
    52	  at: the principle set plus one typedef per definition document type.
    53	- **owner** — the role that approves changes to a definition; named in
    54	  every definition's frontmatter.
    55	- **definition chain** — the six linked definitions of good for one
    56	  artifact type; required before instances are authored or rewritten.
    57	- **keeper** — a corpus record whose action is keep-rewrite; rewritten
    58	  forward through its type's approved chain, never used as-is.
    59	- **rewrite-forward** — the default for keepers: re-author to the
    60	  approved standard; repair-in-place only for records already at the bar.
    61	- **rebaseline** — Phase 1 of the re-founding arc: the active tree comes
    62	  to hold only chain-conforming records; retired mass moves to the
    63	  archive.
    64	- **scope** (of a principle set) — the level the set governs and whose
    65	  context it loads into: working (every activity) or architecture (the
    66	  designed system).
    67	- **transcript** — the runtime log of turns; unscoped, not a governed
    68	  artifact, never loaded into context.
    69	- **conversation** — a scoped, bounded discussion attached to exactly one
    70	  anchor; every conversation belongs to a process.
    71	- **anchor** — the governed record a conversation attaches to: a session
    72	  record, a review record, or a work item; carries the conversation's
    73	  state across transcript boundaries.
    74	- **conversation type** — discovery (anchor: a session record), review
    75	  (anchor: a review record and its outcomes), or work (anchor: a work
    76	  item).
    77	- **session record** — the anchor record of a discovery conversation:
    78	  outcome, produced and revised lists, open threads, select quotes.
    79	- **review** — one bounded conversation in which the authority decides
    80	  on presented material. Replaces "sitting".
    81	- **review record** — the anchor record of a review: the material
    82	  presented and the outcomes applied; each decision traces in the
    83	  changed artifacts' Document History, never in a standing ledger.
    84	- **park** — the failsafe for work that cannot pass review within its
    85	  round cap: set aside with a filed finding.
    86	- **round cap** — the declared maximum review rounds before a loop's
    87	  failsafe exit fires.
    88	- **action** — the approved choice for one record: keep-rewrite, keep,
    89	  retire, or terminal, with its target.
    90	- **authority-call** — a row marker on a migration-plan row awaiting a
    91	  decision from the authority; not an action — the row has no effect and
    92	  is out of scope for any run until ruled.
    93	- **action table** — the table of records and their actions; approved row
    94	  by row or in blocks at a review. Drives any bulk record change.
    95	- **close-out** — the mechanical execution of the migration plan's
    96	  pre-decided retire and terminal actions: snapshot, delete, archive
    97	  move, a loud post-check, and the branch promotion; no review loop.
    98	  All stages run consecutively at cut-over.

    39	unanswered before its default applies; required for any process whose
    40	steps carry `asks`).

    43	
    44	1. **Purpose** — one short paragraph.
    45	2. **Guiding statement** (optional) — directs judgment across the whole
    46	   process; the compiler copies it into every rendering.
    47	3. **Outcomes** — each names the step or check that witnesses it.
    48	4. **Roles** — roles and their accountability; role files carry identity,
    49	   never sequencing.

    51	   edited by hand.

    53	   primitives) inline; every structured shape is a `$ref` to a defined
    54	   type with an explicit source: `from:` is a relative link to the
    55	   defining file, or `pkg:<package>/<type>` when the type lives in
    56	   another package and is fetched through that package's contract tool
    57	   (e.g. `shop-knowledge schema session-record`). Every distinct `$ref`
    58	   carries `from:` at least once; the linter verifies local sources
    59	   define the referenced type. No structured shape is ever defined here.
    60	   A value may declare `initial` — its value at run start.

    63	   cites its clause or is deleted.

    69	## The steps section
    70	
    71	Top-level keys: `start` (first step id); optional `parameters` (data
    72	values supplied at instantiation rather than produced by any step);
    73	optional `result` (the data value a run returns — the artifact, not a
    74	status record; omit only when the outcomes pin the run's value). `end`
    75	is the reserved terminator id for `next`. Each step:

    77	- `id`, `name`; `run-by` — `{role, execution: agent}`,
    78	  `{role, execution: human}` (a role a person holds, e.g. an authority review), or `{execution: runtime}`; `fresh-context: true` where a role
    79	  must not carry memory between runs.
    80	- `inputs` / `outputs` — lists of declared data names; the typed contract
    81	  is the isolation mechanism (a step reads only what it lists).
    82	- Agent and human steps carry `prompt` — **the only prose allowed in a
    83	  step** (for a human step it is the review's ask).
    84	- Runtime steps carry `set` (CEL assignments to data values or their
    85	  fields), `run` (command templates
    86	  with `${...}` interpolation from typed inputs; `atomic: true` binds the
    87	  lines into one all-or-nothing act), or `branches`.
    88	- `checks` — CEL expressions over declared data.
    89	- Routing: `next`, or `branches` of `{label, when (CEL), next}` rows plus
    90	  one `else`. **Every loop declares its exits as labeled branch rows** —
    91	  a reached-state success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
    92	- `asks` — optional list of role ids the step may put an ask to (the

    97	  a judgment the step's role owes. Steps that frame or plan ask early;

   104	  conversation invoked this way is a branched conversation: the child's

   107	## Run lifecycle
   108	
   109	A run is one execution of a process, anchored to a work item in the
   110	registry. Run states: `running`, `held`, `done`, `cancelled`.
   111	
   112	- **Hold** pauses a run: the current step and every data value persist in

   114	  resumed at its recorded step or cancelled with a reason — never
   115	  silently dropped.

   117	  inside the window is held by the runtime. Unfinished work parks itself
   118	  with a named resume point; nothing dangles in the lead repo.
   119	- **Ask** holds a run the same way, with the ask recorded on the anchor
   120	  and routed to whoever fills the role it names — a person or an agent;

   122	  step with the ask in its inputs, in a fresh context loaded from the

   130	- **Cancel** closes the run's work item with a reason and files the

   146	value — and every loop declares its exit. **Consequence on failure:** it

# Cold-read screen: basis/types/ask.md (version 1) and process-definition typedef v4 ask clauses

Read in the prescribed order; nothing else opened except the compiled principles rendering.

## Verdict: findings

## Required changes, most important first

1. **The ask-resume-ask loop has no declared exit** (no-orphan-activities, second clause). `ask-cap` bounds one unanswered ask, but nothing bounds how many asks a step may return: a step that resumes "with the ask in its inputs" may return another ask, hold again, and so on without limit. Required: the typedef states a cap on asks per step per run (or "one ask per checkpoint; a second ask from the same step resumes on its default"), and the checklist row "every ask names a default and a checkpoint" gains that cap.

2. **The resumed step's `ask` input has no declared data name.** The typedef says the run "resumes at the asking step with the ask in its inputs", but `inputs` are "lists of declared data names", the Data section says "every structured shape is a `$ref` to a defined type with an explicit source", and the Commitment says a definition compiles only when "every `$ref` resolves". Nothing says which data value holds the ask, so no process carrying `asks` can declare its inputs and compile. Required: either a reserved data name the runtime fills (stated in §The steps section) or a rule that a process with `asks` declares an `ask` value (`$ref: ask`, `from: ../types/ask.md`) that every asking step lists in its inputs.

3. **What happens at the cap is under-specified in ask.md.** The typedef says the run "resumes on the default with the ask marked `defaulted`". ask.md's `default` is "what the asker will do if unanswered at the cap" — a plan, not an answer value — so on resume `answer` is empty and `resolution` is `defaulted`, and the step is expected to act on `default`. ask.md does not say this; it also says the runtime "re-enters the step with the `answer` filled", which is false on the defaulted path.
